record_identity.title: Cline prompt-injection and cache-poisoning chain enabled unauthorized npm package publication

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Cline prompt-injection and cache-poisoning chain enabled unauthorized npm package publication
incident_identity.date_basis: Cline's postmortem and GitHub advisory identify 17 February 2026 as the unauthorised npm publication date.

summary: An attacker used a prompt-injection and GitHub Actions cache-poisoning chain associated with Cline's Claude-powered issue triage to obtain an npm token and publish an unauthorised `cline@2.3.0` package.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The researcher's reconstruction shows that untrusted issue text could direct the triage agent to execute code, after which shared cache scope could bridge into privileged release workflows. Cline's postmortem states that an attacker used the chain to steal an npm token and publish version 2.3.0 with a postinstall script for OpenClaw. Cline deprecated the version, revoked credentials and reported no evidence that OpenClaw itself was malicious or that user data was exposed.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: Untrusted issue content crossed into a tool-enabled workflow and then propagated through shared infrastructure into release authority. The model interaction was one necessary link; cache design, token scope and release configuration were independently necessary.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The case demonstrates that AI issue-triage agents must be isolated from shared build state and publication credentials, because prompt injection can become supply-chain authority through ordinary CI/CD mechanisms.
assessment_boundaries: The original researcher tested a mirror and states that a different actor weaponised the published technique against Cline.
The evidence does not support attributing the entire chain to Claude or treating OpenClaw as malicious.
